blocks.prompt: 4. Find the equation of lines represented by \(x^{2} + 2xy\sec\alpha + y^{2} = 0\) and also find measure of the angle between them. (Problems 1-5)
blocks.explanation:
A homogeneous second degree equation with a letter \(\alpha\) in the middle coefficient.
Splitting the middle term is not convenient here, so we use the ready lines of Theorem 8.
Plan: read \(a\), \(h\), \(b\); simplify \(\sqrt{h^{2} - ab}\) with \(\sec^{2}\alpha - 1 = \tan^{2}\alpha\); write the lines; then the angle formula.
steps:
Given: \(x^{2} + 2xy\sec\alpha + y^{2} = 0\).
To find: the two lines and the angle between them.
Method: Theorem 8 gives the lines \(by + x(h \pm \sqrt{h^{2}-ab}) = 0\); Section 5.9 gives \(\tan\theta = \dfrac{2\sqrt{h^{2}-ab}}{a + b}\). We take \(\alpha\) as an acute angle (\(0 < \alpha < 90^{\circ}\)), so \(\tan\alpha > 0\).

Read \(a\), \(h\), \(b\)
\[a = 1,\quad 2h = 2\sec\alpha \Rightarrow h = \sec\alpha,\quad b = 1\]
Why: \(h\) is half the coefficient of \(xy\).

Simplify the square root
\[h^{2} - ab = \sec^{2}\alpha - 1 = \tan^{2}\alpha\]
\[\sqrt{h^{2} - ab} = \tan\alpha\]
Why: the identity \(1 + \tan^{2}\alpha = \sec^{2}\alpha\). Since \(\tan^{2}\alpha \ge 0\), the lines are always real.

Write the two lines
\[y + x(\sec\alpha + \tan\alpha) = 0\]
\[y + x(\sec\alpha - \tan\alpha) = 0\]
Why: put \(b = 1\), \(h = \sec\alpha\) and \(\sqrt{h^{2}-ab} = \tan\alpha\) in \(by + x(h \pm \sqrt{h^{2}-ab}) = 0\).

Solve for \(y\)
\[y = -(\sec\alpha + \tan\alpha)x\]
\[y = -(\sec\alpha - \tan\alpha)x\]
\[\text{i.e. } y = x(-\sec\alpha \pm \tan\alpha)\]
Why: move the \(x\)-term to the right side.

Angle between the lines
\[\tan\theta = \dfrac{2\tan\alpha}{1 + 1} = \tan\alpha\]
\[\theta = \alpha\]
Why: formula (iv) with \(a + b = 2\). (For a general \(\alpha\) the acute angle has \(\tan\theta = |\tan\alpha|\).)

Check:
\[m_{1}m_{2} = (\sec\alpha + \tan\alpha)(\sec\alpha - \tan\alpha)\]
\[= \sec^{2}\alpha - \tan^{2}\alpha = 1 = \dfrac{a}{b} \;\checkmark\]
\[m_{1} + m_{2} = -2\sec\alpha = -\dfrac{2h}{b} \;\checkmark\]
Why: the sum and product of the slopes agree with Section 5.9.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The answer key (entry 4) prints \(y = x(\tan\alpha \pm \sec\alpha)\) and \(90^{\circ}\). Both are wrong. Those slopes multiply to \(\tan^{2}\alpha - \sec^{2}\alpha = -1\), and their joint equation is \(y^{2} - 2xy\tan\alpha - x^{2} = 0\), not the given one. The given equation has \(a + b = 2 \ne 0\), so its lines are not perpendicular. Correct: \(y = x(-\sec\alpha \pm \tan\alpha)\), angle \(\theta = \alpha\) (\(\tan\theta = \tan\alpha\)).
